title: Never was I not
hookLine: Arjuna drops his bow, and Krishna's first teaching is that no one here truly ends
carry: the atman was never born and never dies
tomorrow: why would one verse say 'self' again and again?

cards: A word never met before: nasam. Can a known root crack it? Split it: na, not, and asam, from as, to be, the root under asmi.
I was not. The guess holds. Now the scene where that word is said.
A chariot stands between two armies. Arjuna has put down his bow, told his friend Krishna he will not fight, and gone silent. The text says Krishna answers him as if smiling.

teach.h: NEVER WAS I NOT, NOR YOU.
teach.b: Here's the first half, Bhagavad Gita 2.12: na tv evaham jatu nasam, na tvam neme janadhipah. Evaham hides aham, I. Nasam: I was not.
Neme is na plus ime: not these. Never was I not, nor you, nor these lords of men. Then: na chaiva na bhavishyamah sarve vayam atah param.
Nor will we ever cease to be, all of us.

Watch the small words: aham, I; tvam, you; ime, these, the kings across the field; then vayam, we. Krishna starts with himself, adds his friend, adds the very people Arjuna can't bear to kill, and closes the circle.

And this is the heart of the first thing Krishna teaches in the whole Gita. One verse earlier he has said: you grieve for those who need no grief. Arjuna is grieving people still standing in front of him.
Krishna's answer: what you grieve for is not what dies.
In each of them, and in you, is the atman, the self, never born and never ending.

teach.h: NOT KILLED WHEN THE BODY IS.
teach.b: The verses that follow say it plainly: as one passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, the self passes on to another body; it is not killed when the body is killed.

teach.h: DEATH IS NOT THE END OF YOU.
teach.b: This is one of the most basic Hindu beliefs: the real you is not the body, and death is not the end of you. It's one reason many families have verses from this chapter read when someone is dying or has died.
The schools differ on the details, whether every self is finally one or each is eternal in its own right, but all hear the same comfort: never was I not, nor you, nor these.

how: Many Hindu families have verses from Gita chapter two read when someone is dying or has died; some Hindus learn 2.12 by heart, saying it line by line after a teacher.

the opposite: never was I not, nor you, nor these, nor will we cease to be. the atman outlives the body.

games.q: at a grandparent's memorial, a younger cousin asks why everyone keeps reading the Gita. what's the plain answer from 2.12?
o: it teaches that the self in each of us, atman, was never born and doesn't die with the body.
it's just the most well-known poem, so people read it out of habit.
it says the person will come back exactly as they were.
games.why: Krishna's first teaching: never was I not, nor you, nor these. the body ends; the atman doesn't. that's why families turn to these verses.

practice: Say four small words out loud, slowly, one to a breath: aham, I; tvam, you; ime, these; vayam, we.
On aham, feel your own breath; on tvam, bring one person you love to mind; on ime, the people around you today; on vayam, all of you together.
Then let the words go, keep breathing, and rest in the line beneath them: never was I not, nor you.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words, and four of them today: aham, I; tvam, you; ime, these; vayam, we. Who's in the room.

orig.note: Sanskrit: aham, I; the first of the small words in Gita 2.12, hidden in evaham.
